/* ─── LOADING SCREEN ─── */
function LoadingScreen({ onFinished }: { onFinished: () => void }) {
  const [progress, setProgress] = useState(0);
  const [phase, setPhase] = useState<"loading" | "revealing" | "done">("loading");

  useEffect(() => {
    // Smooth progress animation over ~1.8s
    const start = performance.now();
    const duration = 1800;
    let raf: number;

    function tick(now: number) {
      const elapsed = now - start;
      const t = Math.min(elapsed / duration, 1);
      // Ease-out cubic for satisfying feel
      const eased = 1 - Math.pow(1 - t, 3);
      setProgress(Math.round(eased * 100));

      if (t < 1) {
        raf = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
      } else {
        // Begin reveal phase
        setPhase("revealing");
        setTimeout(() => {
          setPhase("done");
          onFinished();
        }, 600);
      }
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    return () => cancelAnimationFrame(raf);
  }, [onFinished]);

  if (phase === "done") return null;

  return (
    <div className={`loading-screen ${phase === "revealing" ? "is-revealing" : ""}`}>
      {/* Ambient orbs */}
      <div className="loader-orb loader-orb-1" />
      <div className="loader-orb loader-orb-2" />
      <div className="loader-orb loader-orb-3" />

      {/* Particle field */}
      <div className="loader-particles">
        {Array.from({ length: 30 }, (_, i) => (
          <span
            key={i}
            className="loader-particle"
            style={{
              left: `${(i * 37.7 + 11) % 100}%`,
              top: `${(i * 61.3 + 7) % 100}%`,
              animationDelay: `${(i * 0.37) % 3}s`,
              animationDuration: `${2 + ((i * 0.53) % 3)}s`,
            }}
          />
        ))}
      </div>

      {/* Central content */}
      <div className="loader-content">
        {/* Animated rings */}
        <div className="loader-rings">
          <div className="loader-ring loader-ring-outer" />
          <div className="loader-ring loader-ring-middle" />
          <div className="loader-ring loader-ring-inner" />
        </div>

        {/* Brand icon */}
        <div className="loader-brand">
          <div className="loader-brand-icon">
            <Icon name="spark" size={28} />
          </div>
          <span className="loader-brand-text">synapse<span>.</span></span>
        </div>

        {/* Progress bar */}
        <div className="loader-progress">
          <div className="loader-progress-track">
            <div
              className="loader-progress-fill"
              style={{ width: `${progress}%` }}
            />
            <div
              className="loader-progress-glow"
              style={{ left: `${progress}%` }}
            />
          </div>
          <span className="loader-progress-text">{progress}%</span>
        </div>

        {/* Status text */}
        <p className="loader-status">
          {progress < 30
            ? "Initializing your study space…"
            : progress < 60
              ? "Loading AI tools…"
              : progress < 90
                ? "Preparing workspace…"
                : "Almost ready…"}
        </p>
      </div>

      {/* Scan line */}
      <div className="loader-scanline" />
    </div>
  );
}

    const card = e.currentTarget;
    const rect = card.getBoundingClientRect();
    const x = e.clientX - rect.left;
    const y = e.clientY - rect.top;
    card.style.setProperty("--glow-x", `${x}px`);
    card.style.setProperty("--glow-y", `${y}px`);
  }, []);

title: redirect
description: API Reference for the redirect function.
related:
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/permanentRedirect
    - app/guides/server-actions
---

The `redirect` function allows you to redirect the user to another URL. `redirect` can be used while rendering in [Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data).

When used in a [streaming context](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#streaming), this will insert a meta tag to emit the redirect on the client side. In a Server Action, `redirect` performs a client-side navigation when JavaScript is available. For progressive enhancement form submissions, it serves a 303 HTTP redirect response. Otherwise, it serves a 307 HTTP redirect response.

If a resource doesn't exist, you can use the [`notFound` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/not-found) instead.

## Reference

### Parameters

The `redirect` function accepts two arguments:

```js
redirect(path, type)
```

| Parameter | Type                                                          | Description                                                 |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `path`    | `string`                                                      | The URL to redirect to. Can be a relative or absolute path. |
| `type`    | `'replace'` (default) or `'push'` (default in Server Actions) | The type of redirect to perform.                            |

By default, `redirect` will use `push` (adding a new entry to the browser history stack) in [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) and `replace` (replacing the current URL in the browser history stack) everywhere else. You can override this behavior by specifying the `type` parameter.

The `RedirectType` object contains the available options for the `type` parameter.

```ts
import { redirect, RedirectType } from 'next/navigation'
```

| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| [`redirect`](#redirect-function)                              | Redirect user after a mutation or event           | Server Components, Server Functions, Route Handlers | 307 (Temporary) or 303 (Server Action) |
| [`permanentRedirect`](#permanentredirect-function)            | Redirect user after a mutation or event           | Server Components, Server Functions, Route Handlers | 308 (Permanent)                        |
| [`useRouter`](#userouter-hook)                                | Perform a client-side navigation                  | Event Handlers in Client Components                 | N/A                                    |
| [`redirects` in `next.config.js`](#redirects-in-nextconfigjs) | Redirect an incoming request based on a path      | `next.config.js` file                               | 307 (Temporary) or 308 (Permanent)     |

## `redirect` function

The `redirect` function allows you to redirect the user to another URL. You can call `redirect` in [Server Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data).

`redirect` is often used after a mutation or event. For example, creating a post:

```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher
'use server'

import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(id: string) {
```
```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher
  try {
    // Call database
  } catch (error) {
    // Handle errors
  }

  revalidatePath('/posts') // Update cached posts
  redirect(`/post/${id}`) // Navigate to the new post page
}
```

See the [`redirect` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/redirect) for more information.

export default function Home() {
  const [showAuth, setShowAuth] = useState(false);
  const [authMessage, setAuthMessage] = useState("");
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(true);

  const handleLoadingFinished = useCallback(() => {
    setIsLoading(false);
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => {
    const params = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
    const authError = params.get("authError");

    if (authError) {
      const timeout = window.setTimeout(() => {
        setAuthMessage(
          params.get("authMessage") ??
            (authError === "callback"
              ? "OAuth sign-in could not complete. Retry, then check the Supabase and Google redirect URL settings if it happens again."
              : `OAuth sign-in could not complete (${authError}). Check the Supabase and Google provider settings, then try again.`),
        );
        setShowAuth(true);
        window.history.replaceState(null, "", window.location.pathname + window.location.hash);
      }, 0);

      return () => window.clearTimeout(timeout);
    }
  }, []);

  return showAuth ? (
    <LoginPage
      onBack={() => {
        setShowAuth(false);
        setAuthMessage("");
        window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "instant" });
      }}
      initialMessage={authMessage}
    />
  ) : (
    <>
      {isLoading && <LoadingScreen onFinished={handleLoadingFinished} />}
      <LandingPage
        onGetStarted={() => {
          setAuthMessage("");
          setShowAuth(true);
          window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "instant" });
        }}
      />
    </>
  );
}

export function getGroqConfig() {
  const apiKey = process.env.GROQ_API_KEY;

  if (!apiKey) {
    throw new Error("Groq is not configured. Add GROQ_API_KEY to your server environment.");
  }

  return {
    apiKey,
    chatModel: process.env.GROQ_CHAT_MODEL || "llama-3.3-70b-versatile",
  };
}

export async function groqChatCompletion(
  messages: { role: "system" | "user" | "assistant"; content: string }[],
) {
  const { apiKey, chatModel } = getGroqConfig();
  const response = await fetch(`${GROQ_API_URL}/chat/completions`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      Authorization: `******
      "Content-Type": "application/json",
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      model: chatModel,
      messages,
      temperature: 0.3,
      max_tokens: 1200,
    }),
  });

  const payload: unknown = await response.json().catch(() => null);
  if (!response.ok) {
    console.error("Groq chat request failed", response.status, payload);
    throw new Error("Groq could not answer right now. Please try again.");
  }

  const content = (payload as {
    choices?: { message?: { content?: string | null } }[];
  }).choices?.[0]?.message?.content;

  if (!content?.trim()) {
    throw new Error("Groq returned an empty answer. Please try again.");
  }

  return content.trim();
}

export async function groqTranscription(file: File) {
  const { apiKey } = getGroqConfig();
  const body = new FormData();
  body.append("file", file, file.name);
  body.append("model", "whisper-large-v3-turbo");
  body.append("response_format", "json");

  const response = await fetch(`${GROQ_API_URL}/audio/transcriptions`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `****** },
    body,
  });
  const payload: unknown = await response.json().catch(() => null);

  if (!response.ok) {
    console.error("Groq transcription request failed", response.status, payload);
    throw new Error("Groq could not transcribe this recording. Check the file and try again.");
  }

  const text = (payload as { text?: unknown }).text;
  if (typeof text !== "string" || !text.trim()) {
    throw new Error("No speech was detected in this recording.");
  }

  return text.trim();
}

export const instant = false;

export default async function DashboardPage() {
  if (!isSupabaseConfigured()) redirect("/");

  const supabase = await createClient();
  const { data: { user }, error } = await supabase.auth.getUser();

  if (error || !user) redirect("/");


  const metadataName = user.user_metadata.full_name ?? user.user_metadata.name;
  const name =
    typeof metadataName === "string" && metadataName.trim()
      ? metadataName.trim()
      : user.email?.split("@")[0] ?? "Student";

  const avatarUrl = user.user_metadata.avatar_url ?? user.user_metadata.picture;

  return (
    <DashboardHome
      name={name}
      email={user.email ?? ""}
      provider={user.app_metadata.provider === "google" ? "Google" : "Email"}
      avatarUrl={avatarUrl}
    />
  );
}

title: instant
description: Configure instant navigation validation for a route segment.
related:
  title: Next Steps
  description: Learn how to use instant navigations in practice.
  links:
    - app/guides/instant-navigation

---

The `instant` route segment config controls how Next.js validates whether a navigation into this segment would produce an instant UI.

Next.js uses prefetching to preload navigations for all in-app links on the current page. However, client-side data fetching or partially prerendered results from the server can lead to navigations that don't update the UI immediately. To help you build fast-feeling navigations, `instant` lets you tell Next.js what to expect from navigations through the configured segment. For instance, you can indicate that navigations into this segment should produce a UI that renders instantly without waiting on any externally loaded data. You can also indicate that navigations aren't expected to be instant.

When a segment is configured to expect an instant UI, Next.js surfaces any code in your application that would block the navigation from updating the UI immediately. See the [Instant Navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for an end-to-end walkthrough.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - The `instant` export only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled.
> - `instant` cannot be used in Client Components. It will throw an error.
> - Next.js does not perform prefetches in development, so navigations may not feel as instant as they will in production. Validation reflects what will happen during `next start`, where prefetching is enabled.

```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx" switcher
export const instant = true

export default function Page() {
  return <div>...</div>
}
```

```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js" switcher
export const instant = true

export default function Page() {
  return <div>...</div>
}
```

## Reference

The export accepts:

- **`true`**: Opts the segment into validation at whatever level is configured globally (see [Configuring validation defaults](#configuring-validation-defaults)). With the framework defaults, validation runs in development only and surfaces errors in the dev overlay.
- **`false`**: Opts the segment out (see [Disabling instant](#disabling-instant)).
- An **object**: Opts in with additional options. See [`level`](#level).

### `level`

Sets the severity at which validation runs for this segment.

```tsx filename="page.tsx"
export const instant = {
  level: 'warning',
}
```

- **`'warning'`**: Validates in development only. Errors appear in the dev overlay; the build is unaffected.

In the future a validation level that supports validation during build will be supported. Unless you are enabling experimental validation modes there is no need to specify level since the only level available is `"warning"`.

When `level` is omitted (or `instant = true` is used), the segment is validated at whatever level is configured globally — see [Configuring validation defaults](#configuring-validation-defaults).

### Disabling instant

Set `false` on a layout or page to indicate that this segment is allowed to block when navigating to it.

This is useful when a deeper page should be instant but an ancestor can't be. For instance, if a shared layout cannot load instantly but you still want to assert that pages beneath this layout can be navigated to instantly, you can ensure that the pages have `instant = true` while the shared layout has `instant = false`.

```tsx filename="app/tabs/layout.tsx"
export const instant = false
```

```tsx filename="app/tabs/[tab]/page.tsx"
export const instant = true
```

Navigations from outside into a tab are allowed to block at the layout. Navigations between tabs are validated for instant UI.

You don't need to add `false` to ancestors of an instant page just because they do something blocking — a higher-up `instant = true` doesn't force its descendants to validate, and leaving an ancestor unconfigured is fine. Reach for `false` only when you've configured a deeper page as instant and need to exempt navigations that pass through a blocking ancestor.

### Disabling static shell validation

Cache Components also validates that each page in your app produces a non-empty static shell at prerender time. To opt a route out of this validation, ensure the highest `instant` config in the route's tree is `false` — a `false` higher in the tree takes precedence over any deeper `true` for the static-shell check.

Setting `false` on the root layout disables static shell validation for the entire app. Place the `false` as low as possible — only as high as needed to cover the routes you want to opt out — so the rest of the app keeps validating.

## How validation works

`instant` triggers validation at every shared layout boundary in the route. Validation runs during development (on page loads and HMR updates) and surfaces errors in the dev error overlay.

Each error identifies the component that would block navigation. The fix is usually to cache the data with `use cache` or wrap it in a `<Suspense>` boundary.

## How `instant` differs from `ensureStatic`

`instant` validates whether a navigation shows UI immediately. [`ensureStatic`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/ensureStatic) requires selected server-rendered output to be static instead of rendered for each request. A route can be fully static and still block a navigation, for example when a Client Component loads data in the browser.

## Configuring validation defaults

By default (`validationLevel: 'warning'`), Cache Components apps validate every Page and Default segment in development. The `experimental.instantInsights.validationLevel` config tunes this behavior — for example, to limit validation to segments that opt in explicitly via `instant`.

```js filename="next.config.js"
module.exports = {
  experimental: {
    instantInsights: {
      validationLevel: 'warning',
    },
  },
}
```

The supported levels are:

- **`'warning'`** _(framework default)_: Every Page and Default segment is implicitly validated at warning level (dev only).
- **`'manual-warning'`**: Only segments with an explicit `instant` are validated, at warning level (dev only).

Setting `instant = false` on a segment opts it out of validation entirely.

> **Good to know**:
>
> - The framework default may change in future versions to opt users into higher levels of validation. Because this feature is experimental, that change is not considered a breaking change. To pin a specific behavior, set `validationLevel` explicitly.
> - Framework-synthesized error routes (`/_global-error`, `/_not-found`) are excluded from implicit validation. To validate them, opt in explicitly with `instant`.

## Inspecting loading states

The Navigation Inspector is available when Cache Components is enabled:

```js filename="next.config.js"
module.exports = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}
```

Open the Next.js DevTools and select **Navigation Inspector**, then turn on **Pause on navigations**. While the toggle is on:

- Refresh the page to freeze the initial static UI generated for the route, before any dynamic data streams in.
- Click a link to freeze the prefetched UI for the destination route.

When the UI is frozen, click **Resume** to let the current navigation finish. The toggle stays on, so the next refresh or link click pauses too. Turn it off when you are done. Use both page refreshes and link clicks to check that your loading states look right on first visit and on navigation.

## Testing instant navigation

The `@next/playwright` package exports an `instant()` helper that holds back dynamic content while the callback runs against the instant UI. The testing API is available automatically in development. For a production build, enable [`experimental.exposeTestingApiInProductionBuild`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/exposeTestingApiInProductionBuild) in the test build. See the [guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#prevent-regressions-with-e2e-tests) for a full example.

```typescript
import { instant } from '@next/playwright'
```

{/* TODO: remove when fixed and from prod-docs-release */}

## Known issue: shared cookie across projects

The DevTools use a `next-instant-navigation-testing` cookie to hold back dynamic content and freeze the page at the instant UI. Because cookies are scoped to the domain and not the port, running multiple projects on the same domain (typically `localhost`) means the cookie is shared across them and can cause unexpected behavior. Clear the cookie or close the Navigation Inspector panel when switching between projects to avoid issues.

> **Good to know:** This will be fixed as part of stabilizing the feature.

## TypeScript

```tsx
type InstantConfig =
  | true
  | false
  | {
      level?: 'warning'
    }

export const instant: InstantConfig = true
```

To run Synapse locally:

1. **Add your Groq key**  
   Open the project’s `.env.local` file and add these lines, keeping your existing Supabase settings:
   ```env
   GROQ_API_KEY=your-groq-api-key
   GROQ_CHAT_MODEL=llama-3.3-70b-versatile
   ```
   Get the key from your GroqCloud account. Keep it private—don’t add `NEXT_PUBLIC_` or share the key.

2. **Set up the Supabase tables**  
   In Supabase, open **SQL Editor** and run the migration files in `supabase/migrations` in date order:
   - `202606240001_study_notebooks.sql`
   - `202610200001_study_workspace_modules.sql`

   If you already ran the first migration, run only the second one. These migrations enable notebooks, saved chats, notes, flashcards, and quizzes.

3. **Check Supabase authentication**  
   Make sure your Supabase URL and publishable key are set in `.env.local`. If you use Google login, keep the Google provider enabled and the Supabase callback/redirect URLs configured as before.

4. **Start the app**  
   Open PowerShell and run:
   ```powershell
   cd "C:\Users\HarshLocal\Desktop\synapse ai study website"
   npm run dev
   ```
   Then open **http://localhost:3000**. If the app reports missing packages, run `npm install` once from the project folder and restart the dev server.

After signing in, try the **Chat** module without choosing a notebook, or upload a source to use Notes, Flashcards, Quiz, and notebook-specific chat. Restart `npm run dev` after changing `.env.local`.

# officeParser: Universal Office Document Parser & Generator A robust, strictly-typed **Node.js and Browser** library for parsing office files into a rich **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)** and generating high-fidelity output in multiple formats. **Parses:** [`docx`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Open_XML) · [`pptx`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Open_XML) · [`xlsx`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Open_XML) · [`odt`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenDocument) · [`odp`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenDocument) · [`ods`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenDocument) · [`odg`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenDocument) · [`pdf`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PDF) · [`rtf`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rich_Text_Format) · [`csv`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comma-separated_values) · [`md`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markdown) · [`html`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTML) · [`epub`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EPUB) · [`tex`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaTeX) (LaTeX, including Overleaf project zips) **Generates:** `DOCX` · `ODT` · `LaTeX` · `Markdown` · `HTML` · `CSV` · `RTF` · `PDF` · `EPUB` · `Plain Text` · `RAG Chunks` [![npm version](https://badge.fury.io/js/officeparser.svg)](https://badge.fury.io/js/officeparser) [![Total Downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dt/officeparser.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/officeparser) [![Weekly Downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dw/officeparser.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/officeparser) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT) --- ### 🌟 [Live Interactive AST Visualizer & Documentation](https://harshankur.github.io/officeParser/) 🌟 *Upload any office file in your browser: inspect the AST, tweak config, and preview generated output in real-time.* - **AST Visualizer**: Inspect the hierarchical node tree, metadata, and raw content - **Config Configurator**: Tweak options (`ignoreNotes`, `ocr`, `newlineDelimiter`) and see results instantly - **Debugging**: Identify exactly how nodes are interpreted - **Format Specs**: Read detailed specs for the AST structure and all config options --- ### 📝 [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) --- ## What's New in v8 - **Rebuilt PDF text extraction.** PDF is no longer treated as a page of flat lines. Tagged PDFs now yield real `heading` (with correct levels), `table`/`row`/`cell`, `list` and footnote/endnote `note` nodes, and one `paragraph` per paragraph. Untagged PDFs recover the same structure geometrically. Multi-column and float-beside-text pages are read in the correct order (recursive XY-cut), broken and glued words are fixed from inter-fragment spacing, super/subscripts and hyphenated line-breaks are rejoined, rotated text is recovered, and internal links resolve to the target section. `.to('text')` is **layout-faithful by default**, rendering each page as a spatial grid so columns and tables line up like the source. Per-run color/highlight extraction (on by default; set `pdfParserConfig.extractTextColor: false` to skip it) and merged-cell (`colSpan`/`rowSpan`) recovery round it out, and every node carries page geometry (`bounds`). - **Password-protected documents.** Encrypted PDF, OOXML (`docx`/`xlsx`/`pptx`) and ODF (`odt`/`ods`/`odp`/`odg`) open through one unified `password` / `onPassword` option, across parsing, conversion and templating. - **Native DOCX & ODT generation**, plus a **native PDF engine** (`pdfConfig.engine: 'native'`, built on `pdf-lib`) that produces real PDF bytes with no headless browser, in Node and the browser alike. - **Templates / mail-merge** via `OfficeTemplate.render` (fill a DOCX template's `{{placeholders}}`, single or batch), and **ODG parsing** (LibreOffice Draw). - **LaTeX in both directions** (8.1): `.tex` files and Overleaf project zips parse into the same AST as every other format (sections, lists, tables with merged cells, figures, math, footnotes, citations, cross-references, user macros, `beamer` slides), so LaTeX converts to DOCX, ODT, HTML, Markdown and the rest. And `to('tex')` turns any parsed document into LaTeX source that compiles unmodified with pdfLaTeX, XeLaTeX, LuaLaTeX, upLaTeX, pLaTeX and `latex` (the last three through dvipdfmx), presentations included (as `beamer` frames), carrying its images inside the one `.tex` file (or, in bundle mode, as files in a zip). See [LaTeX Support](#latex-support). See the [full changelog](CHANGELOG.md) for the complete list, including breaking changes. --- ## Table of Contents - [What's New in v8](#whats-new-in-v8) - [Install](#install-via-npm) - [Command Line Usage](#command-line-usage) - # Synapse

Synapse is a student study workspace built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Supabase.

## Local setup

1. Install dependencies with `npm install`.
2. Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and fill in your Supabase project URL and publishable key.

4. Add `http://localhost:3000/auth/callback` to the Supabase project's allowed redirect URLs.
5. Start the app with `npm run dev`.

title: redirect
description: API Reference for the redirect function.
related:
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/permanentRedirect
    - app/guides/server-actions
---

The `redirect` function allows you to redirect the user to another URL. `redirect` can be used while rendering in [Server and Client Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data).

When used in a [streaming context](/docs/app/getting-started/linking-and-navigating#streaming), this will insert a meta tag to emit the redirect on the client side. In a Server Action, `redirect` performs a client-side navigation when JavaScript is available. For progressive enhancement form submissions, it serves a 303 HTTP redirect response. Otherwise, it serves a 307 HTTP redirect response.

If a resource doesn't exist, you can use the [`notFound` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/not-found) instead.

## Reference

### Parameters

The `redirect` function accepts two arguments:

```js
redirect(path, type)
```

| Parameter | Type                                                          | Description                                                 |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `path`    | `string`                                                      | The URL to redirect to. Can be a relative or absolute path. |
| `type`    | `'replace'` (default) or `'push'` (default in Server Actions) | The type of redirect to perform.                            |

By default, `redirect` will use `push` (adding a new entry to the browser history stack) in [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) and `replace` (replacing the current URL in the browser history stack) everywhere else. You can override this behavior by specifying the `type` parameter.

The `RedirectType` object contains the available options for the `type` parameter.

```ts
import { redirect, RedirectType } from 'next/navigation'

redirect('/redirect-to', RedirectType.replace)
// or
redirect('/redirect-to', RedirectType.push)
```

The `type` parameter has no effect when used in Server Components.

### Returns

`redirect` does not return a value.

## Behavior

- In Server Actions and Route Handlers, redirect should be called **outside** the `try` block when using `try/catch` statements.
- If you prefer to return a 308 (Permanent) HTTP redirect instead of 307 (Temporary), you can use the [`permanentRedirect` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/permanentRedirect) instead.
- `redirect` throws an error so it should be called **outside** the `try` block when using `try/catch` statements.
- `redirect` can be called in Client Components during the rendering process but not in event handlers. You can use the [`useRouter` hook](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/use-router) instead.
- `redirect` also accepts absolute URLs and can be used to redirect to external links.
- If you'd like to redirect before the render process, use [`next.config.js`](/docs/app/guides/redirecting#redirects-in-nextconfigjs) or [Proxy](/docs/app/guides/redirecting#nextresponseredirect-in-proxy).

## Example

### Server Component

Invoking the `redirect()` function throws a `NEXT_REDIRECT` error and terminates rendering of the route segment in which it was thrown.

```tsx filename="app/team/[id]/page.tsx" switcher
import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'

async function fetchTeam(id: string) {
  const res = await fetch('https://...')
  if (!res.ok) return undefined
  return res.json()
}

export default async function Profile({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ id: string }>
}) {
  const { id } = await params
  const team = await fetchTeam(id)

  if (!team) {
    redirect('/login')
  }

  // ...
}
```

There are a few ways you can handle redirects in Next.js. This page will go through each available option, use cases, and how to manage large numbers of redirects.

<AppOnly>

| API                                                           | Purpose                                           | Where                                               | Status Code                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| [`redirect`](#redirect-function)                              | Redirect user after a mutation or event           | Server Components, Server Functions, Route Handlers | 307 (Temporary) or 303 (Server Action) |
| [`permanentRedirect`](#permanentredirect-function)            | Redirect user after a mutation or event           | Server Components, Server Functions, Route Handlers | 308 (Permanent)                        |
| [`useRouter`](#userouter-hook)                                | Perform a client-side navigation                  | Event Handlers in Client Components                 | N/A                                    |
| [`redirects` in `next.config.js`](#redirects-in-nextconfigjs) | Redirect an incoming request based on a path      | `next.config.js` file                               | 307 (Temporary) or 308 (Permanent)     |
| [`NextResponse.redirect`](#nextresponseredirect-in-proxy)     | Redirect an incoming request based on a condition | Proxy                                               | Any                                    |

</AppOnly>

<PagesOnly>

| API                                                           | Purpose                                           | Where                 | Status Code                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| [`useRouter`](#userouter-hook)                                | Perform a client-side navigation                  | Components            | N/A                                |
| [`redirects` in `next.config.js`](#redirects-in-nextconfigjs) | Redirect an incoming request based on a path      | `next.config.js` file | 307 (Temporary) or 308 (Permanent) |
| [`NextResponse.redirect`](#nextresponseredirect-in-proxy)     | Redirect an incoming request based on a condition | Proxy                 | Any                                |

</PagesOnly>

## `redirect` function

The `redirect` function allows you to redirect the user to another URL. You can call `redirect` in [Server Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data).

`redirect` is often used after a mutation or event. For example, creating a post:

```ts filename="app/actions.ts" switcher
'use server'

import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(id: string) {
  try {
    // Call database
  } catch (error) {
    // Handle errors
  }

  revalidatePath('/posts') // Update cached posts
  redirect(`/post/${id}`) // Navigate to the new post page
}
```

```js filename="app/actions.js" switcher

import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'

export async function createPost(id) {
  try {
    // Call database
  } catch (error) {
    // Handle errors
  }

  revalidatePath('/posts') // Update cached posts
  redirect(`/post/${id}`) // Navigate to the new post page
}
```

> **Good to know**:
>
> - In a Server Action, `redirect` performs a client-side navigation when JavaScript is available. Without JavaScript, the form submission uses a 303 (See Other). In other contexts, `redirect` uses a 307 (Temporary Redirect).
> - `redirect` throws an error so it should be called **outside** the `try` block when using `try/catch` statements.
> - `redirect` can be called in Client Components during the rendering process but not in event handlers. You can use the [`useRouter` hook](#userouter-hook) instead.
> - `redirect` also accepts absolute URLs and can be used to redirect to external links.
> - If you'd like to redirect before the render process, use [`next.config.js`](#redirects-in-nextconfigjs) or [Proxy](#nextresponseredirect-in-proxy).

See the [`redirect` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/redirect) for more information.

The `permanentRedirect` function allows you to **permanently** redirect the user to another URL. You can call `permanentRedirect` in [Server Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data).

--- title: instant description: Configure instant navigation validation for a route segment. related: title: Next Steps description: Learn how to use instant navigations in practice. links: - app/guides/instant-navigation - app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/ensureStatic - app/getting-started/caching - app/getting-started/revalidating - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache --- The `instant` route segment config controls how Next.js validates whether a navigation into this segment would produce an instant UI. Next.js uses prefetching to preload navigations for all in-app links on the current page. However, client-side data fetching or partially prerendered results from the server can lead to navigations that don't update the UI immediately. To help you build fast-feeling navigations, `instant` lets you tell Next.js what to expect from navigations through the configured segment. For instance, you can indicate that navigations into this segment should produce a UI that renders instantly without waiting on any externally loaded data. You can also indicate that navigations aren't expected to be instant. When a segment is configured to expect an instant UI, Next.js surfaces any code in your application that would block the navigation from updating the UI immediately. See the [Instant Navigation guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation) for an end-to-end walkthrough. > **Good to know**: > > - The `instant` export only works when [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) is enabled. > - `instant` cannot be used in Client Components. It will throw an error. > - Next.js does not perform prefetches in development, so navigations may not feel as instant as they will in production. Validation reflects what will happen during `next start`, where prefetching is enabled. ```tsx filename="layout.tsx | page.tsx" switcher export const instant = true export default function Page() { return
...
} ``` ```jsx filename="layout.js | page.js" switcher export const instant = true export default function Page() { return
...
} ``` ## Reference The export accepts: - **`true`**: Opts the segment into validation at whatever level is configured globally (see [Configuring validation defaults](#configuring-validation-defaults)). With the framework defaults, validation runs in development only and surfaces errors in the dev overlay. - **`false`**: Opts the segment out (see [Disabling instant](#disabling-instant)). - An **object**: Opts in with additional options. See [`level`](#level). ### `level` Sets the severity at which validation runs for this segment. ```tsx filename="page.tsx" export const instant = { level: 'warning', } ``` - **`'warning'`**: Validates in development only. Errors appear in the dev overlay; the build is unaffected. In the future a validation level that supports validation during build will be supported. Unless you are enabling experimental validation modes there is no need to specify level since the only level available is `"warning"`. When `level` is omitted (or `instant = true` is used), the segment is validated at whatever level is configured globally — see [Configuring validation defaults](#configuring-validation-defaults). ### Disabling instant Set `false` on a layout or page to indicate that this segment is allowed to block when navigating to it. This is useful when a deeper page should be instant but an ancestor can't be. For instance, if a shared layout cannot load instantly but you still want to assert that pages beneath this layout can be navigated to instantly, you can ensure that the pages have `instant = true` while the shared layout has `instant = false`. ```tsx filename="app/tabs/layout.tsx" export const instant = false ``` ```tsx filename="app/tabs/[tab]/page.tsx" export const instant = true ``` Navigations from outside into a tab are allowed to block at the layout. Navigations between tabs are validated for instant UI. You don't need to add `false` to ancestors of an instant page just because they do something blocking — a higher-up `instant = true` doesn't force its descendants to validate, and leaving an ancestor unconfigured is fine. Reach for `false` only when you've configured a deeper page as instant and need to exempt navigations that pass through a blocking ancestor. ### Disabling static shell validation Cache Components also validates that each page in your app produces a non-empty static shell at prerender time. To opt a route out of this validation, ensure the highest `instant` config in the route's tree is `false` — a `false` higher in the tree takes precedence over any deeper `true` for the static-shell check. Setting `false` on the root layout disables static shell validation for the entire app. Place the `false` as low as possible — only as high as needed to cover the routes you want to opt out — so the rest of the app keeps validating. ## How validation works `instant` triggers validation at every shared layout boundary in the route. Validation runs during development (on page loads and HMR updates) and surfaces errors in the dev error overlay. Each error identifies the component that would block navigation. The fix is usually to cache the data with `use cache` or wrap it in a `` boundary. ## How `instant` differs from `ensureStatic` `instant` validates whether a navigation shows UI immediately. [`ensureStatic`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/ensureStatic) requires selected server-rendered output to be static instead of rendered for each request. A route can be fully static and still block a navigation, for example when a Client Component loads data in the browser. ## Configuring validation defaults By default (`validationLevel: 'warning'`), Cache Components apps validate every Page and Default segment in development. The `experimental.instantInsights.validationLevel` config tunes this behavior — for example, to limit validation to segments that opt in explicitly via `instant`. ```js filename="next.config.js" module.exports = { experimental: { instantInsights: { validationLevel: 'warning', }, }, } ``` The supported levels are: - **`'warning'`** _(framework default)_: Every Page and Default segment is implicitly validated at warning level (dev only). - **`'manual-warning'`**: Only segments with an explicit `instant` are validated, at warning level (dev only). Setting `instant = false` on a segment opts it out of validation entirely. > **Good to know**: > > - The framework default may change in future versions to opt users into higher levels of validation. Because this feature is experimental, that change is not considered a breaking change. To pin a specific behavior, set `validationLevel` explicitly. > - Framework-synthesized error routes (`/_global-error`, `/_not-found`) are excluded from implicit validation. To validate them, opt in explicitly with `instant`. ## Inspecting loading states The Navigation Inspector is available when Cache Components is enabled: ```js filename="next.config.js" module.exports = { cacheComponents: true, } ``` Open the Next.js DevTools and select **Navigation Inspector**, then turn on **Pause on navigations**. While the toggle is on: - Refresh the page to freeze the initial static UI generated for the route, before any dynamic data streams in. - Click a link to freeze the prefetched UI for the destination route. When the UI is frozen, click **Resume** to let the current navigation finish. The toggle stays on, so the next refresh or link click pauses too. Turn it off when you are done. Use both page refreshes and link clicks to check that your loading states look right on first visit and on navigation. ## Testing instant navigation The `@next/playwright` package exports an `instant()` helper that holds back dynamic content while the callback runs against the instant UI. The testing API is available automatically in development. For a production build, enable [`experimental.exposeTestingApiInProductionBuild`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/exposeTestingApiInProductionBuild) in the test build. See the [guide](/docs/app/guides/instant-navigation#prevent-regressions-with-e2e-tests) for a full example. ```typescript import { instant } from '@next/playwright' ``` {/* TODO: remove when fixed and from prod-docs-release */} ## Known issue: shared cookie across projects The DevTools use a `next-instant-navigation-testing` cookie to hold back dynamic content and freeze the page at the instant UI. Because cookies are scoped to the domain and not the port, running multiple projects on the same domain (typically `localhost`) means the cookie is shared across them and can cause unexpected behavior. Clear the cookie or close the Navigation Inspector panel when switching between projects to avoid issues. > **Good to know:** This will be fixed as part of stabilizing the feature. ## TypeScript ```tsx type InstantConfig = | true | false | { level?: 'warning' } export const instant: InstantConfig = true ``` ## Version History | Version | Changes | | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `v16.3.0` | `instant` export stabilized, replacing `unstable_instant` (Cache Components only). |

To run Synapse locally:

1. **Add your Groq key**  
   Open the project’s `.env.local` file and add these lines, keeping your existing Supabase settings:
   ```env
   GROQ_API_KEY=your-groq-api-key
   GROQ_CHAT_MODEL=llama-3.3-70b-versatile
   ```
   Get the key from your GroqCloud account. Keep it private—don’t add `NEXT_PUBLIC_` or share the key.

2. **Set up the Supabase tables**  
   In Supabase, open **SQL Editor** and run the migration files in `supabase/migrations` in date order:
   - `202606240001_study_notebooks.sql`
   - `202610200001_study_workspace_modules.sql`

   If you already ran the first migration, run only the second one. These migrations enable notebooks, saved chats, notes, flashcards, and quizzes.

3. **Check Supabase authentication**  
   Make sure your Supabase URL and publishable key are set in `.env.local`. If you use Google login, keep the Google provider enabled and the Supabase callback/redirect URLs configured as before.

4. **Start the app**  
   Open PowerShell and run:
   ```powershell
   cd "C:\Users\HarshLocal\Desktop\synapse ai study website"
   npm run dev
   ```
   Then open **http://localhost:3000**. If the app reports missing packages, run `npm install` once from the project folder and restart the dev server.

After signing in, try the **Chat** module without choosing a notebook, or upload a source to use Notes, Flashcards, Quiz, and notebook-specific chat. Restart `npm run dev` after changing `.env.local`.

<overview>
Synapse is a student study workspace built with Next.js, Supabase, and Groq. The current request is a dashboard/landing redesign, persistent local task management, notebook-specific workflows, chat citations and actions, and complete removal of voice/podcast features. Work on this newest request is **in progress and unvalidated**; continue from the partially edited files while preserving recent changes already present in the project.
</overview>

<history>
1. The user established Synapse’s vision: a free student workspace that combines study tools, notebook organization, and time management.
   - The project directory is `C:\Users\HarshLocal\Desktop\synapse ai study website`.
   - The frontend uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Supabase; Groq is the requested AI provider.

2. Earlier work built authentication, dashboard/theme support, source ingestion, and study tools.
   - Groq was added for chat and video/audio transcription; `officeparser` was installed with `--ignore-scripts`.
   - Supabase migrations were created for notebooks, chat, notes, flashcards, and quizzes with user-scoped RLS.
   - A previous task added source-optional chat, notes, flashcards and quizzes, quiz remediation, sign-in redirects, and a mascot animation. Builds and TypeScript checks passed at that time.

3. The user returned with a larger redesign request:
   - Create a minimalist/TurboLearn-style dashboard with rounded Feedback and Upgrade buttons; center the animated computer above the “What do you want to learn?” heading; redesign the search/input bar; add recent activity and a Lessons section.
   - Keep only five recent notebooks on Home, retain the full library in sidebar Notebooks, and let each notebook open a workspace for its Chat, Notes, Flashcards, and Quiz.
   - Add a Notion-style task manager with localStorage key `synapse_tasks`, filters, priority/deadline/status, and a dashboard agenda widget.
   - Render AI citations as interactive chips and add Copy and Save to Notes actions under assistant answers.
   - Remove mic/record/voice and podcast features everywhere, including the landing-page podcast demo, waveform, FAQ, and comparison table.

4. Work on the current request began, but was interrupted by the request to summarize.
   - Inspected the current project and found substantial recent user changes beyond the earlier version, including `CustomSelect`, local notebook fallbacks, and an interactive orange mascot. These must be preserved.
   - Started edits in `dashboard-home.tsx` for the task manager, folders, header actions, and dedicated full-library/Tasks views.
   - No current-request changes have yet been validated; several requested parts remain incomplete.
</history>

- The Home layout is still the old composition: mascot is not centered above the heading; search placeholder/layout and recent banner are unchanged; Lessons still displays the full notebook list; no “Today’s Agenda & Deadlines” widget exists.
- Notebook selection still opens Chat, but a dedicated notebook workspace with module tabs has not been added.

**Previously completed features remain in the project**, including Groq chat/ingestion endpoints, notes/flashcard/quiz generation, quiz feedback, existing Supabase migrations, landing/dashboard auth redirects, and prior dashboard modules. [{"role":"system","content":"Task: Judge whether an AI coding assistant satisfied the user's ORIGINAL REQUEST, using the user's FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE as the signal.

You are given four things from a chat with an AI coding assistant:

- **[ORIGINAL REQUEST]**: the user's request(s) that defined the task — the message that started it plus any additional instructions or steering the user sent before the assistant reported the task complete. Treat them together as the single request to satisfy.
- **[ASSISTANT'S FINAL RESPONSE]**: the last thing the assistant actually said on screen before the user replied. This is what the user was looking at when they wrote the follow-up.
- **[TASK SUMMARY]**: the assistant's own summary of what it did when it reported the task complete.
- **[FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE]**: the user's first message after the assistant reported the task complete. This is your primary signal.

## The burden of proof

First handle the narrow `unclear` exception: if the FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE is genuinely unintelligible or visibly truncated so its meaning cannot be recovered, return `unclear`. This exception takes precedence over the satisfied default. The marker `[... section truncated ...]` is a system-applied elision and is not by itself evidence that the message is unintelligible; use `unclear` only if the remaining follow-up content cannot be understood. Do not treat random character fragments with no ordinary meaning as silence or as an implicit approval. A clear message that merely expresses no opinion is not unclear.

The default verdict is **satisfied**. Almost every follow-up is just the user's next piece of work, and that is not a complaint. You may only return `not_satisfied` if you can meet a specific burden of proof, defined below. If you cannot meet it, the answer is `satisfied` — even if you have a hunch the user was unhappy. A hunch is not evidence.

Work through the steps in order. Do not skip ahead to the verdict.

### Step 1 — Name what was delivered

From the TASK SUMMARY and the ASSISTANT'S FINAL RESPONSE, state in a few words the concrete thing that was produced: the file, the answer, the link, the commit, the fix, the slide deck. Be specific about *what it is*.

### Step 2 — Quote a complaint, word for word

Copy the exact words **from the FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE** in which the user asserts that something is wrong, broken, missing, incorrect, or not what they wanted.

Hard rules for this quote:

- It must be **copied verbatim** from the FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE. Never paraphrase, never invent, never quote from anywhere else.
- It must be an **assertion that something is wrong** or a question that semantically challenges the delivered conclusion. A request for work is not a complaint, however it is phrased and however urgent it sounds.
- An information-seeking **question** is not a complaint: "did you open the proposal", "what is the full url", "why does it behave that way". But a question that challenges the delivered conclusion is a complaint: "are you sure this is fixed?", "how can that be complete when the test still fails?", "did you actually answer my question?".
- If no such words exist, leave the quote **empty**. This is the common case and it is a completely normal outcome.

Words that typically carry a real complaint: *not working, doesn't work, still failing, still the same, broken, wrong, that's not what I asked, you missed, I don't see, not like this, undo that, revert that*.

### Step 3 — Does the complaint target what was delivered?

Look at the quote from Step 2 and identify **what thing it is about**. Then answer: is that thing the artifact you named in Step 1, or the outcome this task was supposed to produce?

- Delivered a PowerPoint → *"the power point is not loading, the slides are blank"* → **yes**. That is the delivered artifact.
- Delivered a code fix for an error → *"still same error"* → **yes**. The fix was supposed to end that error.
- Delivered a dashboard using Kusto → *"the metrics should be real time dgrep metrics, not kusto"* → **yes**. The delivered thing was built the wrong way.
- Delivered a metrics analysis → *"why are all my mcp servers failing to connect"* → **no**. MCP servers are a different system that this task never touched.
- Delivered a converted panel → *"i tried cid and tid filter not working"* → **no**, unless the cid/tid filter is itself part of what was delivered.
- Delivered a pushed branch → *"seems like some tests are failing on the PR"* → **no**. That is a newly surfaced problem, not the delivered push.

If the complaint is about a **different component, file, system, or a newly surfaced problem**, answer **no**. A user reporting an unrelated bug is not a user telling you your work was bad.

### Step 4 — Three narrow additions

These three also meet the burden of proof, even without a complaint quote. They are narrow. Do not stretch them.

- **The same failure, again.** The assistant claimed to fix something and the user reports that same thing still failing: *"still same error"*, *"not yet working"*, *"try again"*. The *same* failure repeating — a different or later error does not count.
- **Pushback on a refusal.** The assistant said it could not or would not do the task, and the user insists it can: *"yes you can, you've done this before"*, *"deliver a new ppt if not able to"*.
- **Blocked, partial, or unfinished delivery.** The assistant says an original requirement remains blocked, incomplete, still running, or unanswered, and the follow-up asks about that same requirement. Do not accept a completion claim merely because the assistant used completion language.

In the output, set `same_failure_or_pushback` to true when any Step 4 addition applies, including blocked, partial, or unfinished delivery.

## What is NOT dissatisfaction

Be strict. Every one of these is `satisfied`. Treating any of them as dissatisfaction is the single most common way to get this task wrong:

- **Asking for more work, or the next step** — even on the very same file, artifact, or subject. *"now add tests"*, *"create a bug item and a PR"*, *"generate a word doc with these"*, *"also convert it to PDF"*, *"write the formula into the md"*, *"now submit those review comments"*.
- **Asking for a change to the delivered thing** — renaming labels, adjusting a value, changing formatting, tweaking a date range. Refinement is how normal work proceeds; it is not a verdict on the first attempt.
- **Information-seeking questions** — whether it was done, where it is, what its URL is, why something behaves as it does, whether something is still needed. This does not include a question that disputes the assistant's delivered conclusion.
- **Reporting a different, newly surfaced problem** — a distinct error, a failure in another component, a CI failure that appeared later.
- Applying the same work to a **new target**. *"do the same for the other repo"*.
- Wondering whether the **user themselves** broke something.
- Supplying **details, files, links, or decisions** the assistant asked for, or steering the assistant's next step with new criteria.
- **New constraints never previously mentioned.** If the user never asked for it, its absence is not a failure.
- **Approval followed by another request.** *"good, can you also convert it to PDF"* is approval. The approval is the signal; the request is just the next task.
- **Pasted console output, logs, or a stack trace**, with no sentence from the user saying it is wrong. A paste is the user handing over data for the next step. It counts only if the user's own words identify it as the same failure the assistant claimed to fix.
- A recurring **wake, heartbeat, or scheduling invocation** with no new reaction: *"continue"*, *"wake up"*, *"still working?"*, *"run the scheduled check"*. It is `satisfied`, not `unclear`.
- An interpretable **slash command**. Judge its ordinary meaning: `/review`, `/test`, or `/pr` requests a next action and is `satisfied`; only truly unintelligible text is `unclear`.

The single most common error is this reasoning: *"the user asked for something the assistant hasn't delivered, so the assistant must have fallen short."* **That reasoning is wrong.** A follow-up that requests work is new work. Stop if you catch yourself concluding `not_satisfied` because the assistant "didn't deliver" what the follow-up asks for — that is exactly the trap.

## Verdicts

- **not_satisfied** — Step 2 produced a real verbatim complaint quote **and** Step 3 answered yes; or Step 4 applies. Both halves are required.
- **satisfied** — everything else. This covers explicit approval and, far more often, the user simply moving on to their next piece of work.
- **unclear** — you genuinely cannot tell: the message is unintelligible or truncated, or it plainly reacts to something other than this task.

`unclear` is not for "the user did not express an opinion." Most users never do; that is `satisfied`.

Judge only whether the ORIGINAL REQUEST was satisfied — not the quality or difficulty of any new request.

When you are on the fence, choose `satisfied`. A missed complaint is a small loss; a false accusation is a large one.

## Output

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, filling the steps in order:
{"delivered": "≤15 words naming the thing produced", "complaint_quote": "words copied verbatim from the follow-up, or empty string", "quote_targets_delivered": true | false, "same_failure_or_pushback": true | false, "verdict": "satisfied" | "not_satisfied" | "unclear", "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low", "evidence": "≤15 words"}

`verdict` must be `not_satisfied` if and only if (`complaint_quote` is non-empty AND `quote_targets_delivered` is true) OR `same_failure_or_pushback` is true — unless you answered `unclear`.

messages.content:
Task: Judge whether an AI coding assistant satisfied the user's ORIGINAL REQUEST, using the user's FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE as the signal.

You are given four things from a chat with an AI coding assistant:

- **[ORIGINAL REQUEST]**: the user's request(s) that defined the task — the message that started it plus any additional instructions or steering the user sent before the assistant reported the task complete. Treat them together as the single request to satisfy.
- **[ASSISTANT'S FINAL RESPONSE]**: the last thing the assistant actually said on screen before the user replied. This is what the user was looking at when they wrote the follow-up.
- **[TASK SUMMARY]**: the assistant's own summary of what it did when it reported the task complete.
- **[FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE]**: the user's first message after the assistant reported the task complete. This is your primary signal.

## The burden of proof

First handle the narrow `unclear` exception: if the FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE is genuinely unintelligible or visibly truncated so its meaning cannot be recovered, return `unclear`. This exception takes precedence over the satisfied default. The marker `[... section truncated ...]` is a system-applied elision and is not by itself evidence that the message is unintelligible; use `unclear` only if the remaining follow-up content cannot be understood. Do not treat random character fragments with no ordinary meaning as silence or as an implicit approval. A clear message that merely expresses no opinion is not unclear.

The default verdict is **satisfied**. Almost every follow-up is just the user's next piece of work, and that is not a complaint. You may only return `not_satisfied` if you can meet a specific burden of proof, defined below. If you cannot meet it, the answer is `satisfied` — even if you have a hunch the user was unhappy. A hunch is not evidence.

Work through the steps in order. Do not skip ahead to the verdict.

### Step 1 — Name what was delivered

From the TASK SUMMARY and the ASSISTANT'S FINAL RESPONSE, state in a few words the concrete thing that was produced: the file, the answer, the link, the commit, the fix, the slide deck. Be specific about *what it is*.

### Step 2 — Quote a complaint, word for word

Copy the exact words **from the FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE** in which the user asserts that something is wrong, broken, missing, incorrect, or not what they wanted.

Hard rules for this quote:

- It must be **copied verbatim** from the FOLLOW-UP MESSAGE. Never paraphrase, never invent, never quote from anywhere else.
- It must be an **assertion that something is wrong** or a question that semantically challenges the delivered conclusion. A request for work is not a complaint, however it is phrased and however urgent it sounds.
- An information-seeking **question** is not a complaint: "did you open the proposal", "what is the full url", "why does it behave that way". But a question that challenges the delivered conclusion is a complaint: "are you sure this is fixed?", "how can that be complete when the test still fails?", "did you actually answer my question?".
- If no such words exist, leave the quote **empty**. This is the common case and it is a completely normal outcome.

Words that typically carry a real complaint: *not working, doesn't work, still failing, still the same, broken, wrong, that's not what I asked, you missed, I don't see, not like this, undo that, revert that*.

### Step 3 — Does the complaint target what was delivered?

Look at the quote from Step 2 and identify **what thing it is about**. Then answer: is that thing the artifact you named in Step 1, or the outcome this task was supposed to produce?

- Delivered a PowerPoint → *"the power point is not loading, the slides are blank"* → **yes**. That is the delivered artifact.
- Delivered a code fix for an error → *"still same error"* → **yes**. The fix was supposed to end that error.
- Delivered a dashboard using Kusto → *"the metrics should be real time dgrep metrics, not kusto"* → **yes**. The delivered thing was built the wrong way.
- Delivered a metrics analysis → *"why are all my mcp servers failing to connect"* → **no**. MCP servers are a different system that this task never touched.
- Delivered a converted panel → *"i tried cid and tid filter not working"* → **no**, unless the cid/tid filter is itself part of what was delivered.
- Delivered a pushed branch → *"seems like some tests are failing on the PR"* → **no**. That is a newly surfaced problem, not the delivered push.

If the complaint is about a **different component, file, system, or a newly surfaced problem**, answer **no**. A user reporting an unrelated bug is not a user telling you your work was bad.

### Step 4 — Three narrow additions

These three also meet the burden of proof, even without a complaint quote. They are narrow. Do not stretch them.

- **The same failure, again.** The assistant claimed to fix something and the user reports that same thing still failing: *"still same error"*, *"not yet working"*, *"try again"*. The *same* failure repeating — a different or later error does not count.
- **Pushback on a refusal.** The assistant said it could not or would not do the task, and the user insists it can: *"yes you can, you've done this before"*, *"deliver a new ppt if not able to"*.
- **Blocked, partial, or unfinished delivery.** The assistant says an original requirement remains blocked, incomplete, still running, or unanswered, and the follow-up asks about that same requirement. Do not accept a completion claim merely because the assistant used completion language.

In the output, set `same_failure_or_pushback` to true when any Step 4 addition applies, including blocked, partial, or unfinished delivery.

## What is NOT dissatisfaction

Be strict. Every one of these is `satisfied`. Treating any of them as dissatisfaction is the single most common way to get this task wrong:

- **Asking for more work, or the next step** — even on the very same file, artifact, or subject. *"now add tests"*, *"create a bug item and a PR"*, *"generate a word doc with these"*, *"also convert it to PDF"*, *"write the formula into the md"*, *"now submit those review comments"*.
- **Asking for a change to the delivered thing** — renaming labels, adjusting a value, changing formatting, tweaking a date range. Refinement is how normal work proceeds; it is not a verdict on the first attempt.
- **Information-seeking questions** — whether it was done, where it is, what its URL is, why something behaves as it does, whether something is still needed. This does not include a question that disputes the assistant's delivered conclusion.
- **Reporting a different, newly surfaced problem** — a distinct error, a failure in another component, a CI failure that appeared later.
- Applying the same work to a **new target**. *"do the same for the other repo"*.
- Wondering whether the **user themselves** broke something.
- Supplying **details, files, links, or decisions** the assistant asked for, or steering the assistant's next step with new criteria.
- **New constraints never previously mentioned.** If the user never asked for it, its absence is not a failure.
- **Approval followed by another request.** *"good, can you also convert it to PDF"* is approval. The approval is the signal; the request is just the next task.
- **Pasted console output, logs, or a stack trace**, with no sentence from the user saying it is wrong. A paste is the user handing over data for the next step. It counts only if the user's own words identify it as the same failure the assistant claimed to fix.
- A recurring **wake, heartbeat, or scheduling invocation** with no new reaction: *"continue"*, *"wake up"*, *"still working?"*, *"run the scheduled check"*. It is `satisfied`, not `unclear`.
- An interpretable **slash command**. Judge its ordinary meaning: `/review`, `/test`, or `/pr` requests a next action and is `satisfied`; only truly unintelligible text is `unclear`.

The single most common error is this reasoning: *"the user asked for something the assistant hasn't delivered, so the assistant must have fallen short."* **That reasoning is wrong.** A follow-up that requests work is new work. Stop if you catch yourself concluding `not_satisfied` because the assistant "didn't deliver" what the follow-up asks for — that is exactly the trap.

## Verdicts

- **not_satisfied** — Step 2 produced a real verbatim complaint quote **and** Step 3 answered yes; or Step 4 applies. Both halves are required.
- **satisfied** — everything else. This covers explicit approval and, far more often, the user simply moving on to their next piece of work.
- **unclear** — you genuinely cannot tell: the message is unintelligible or truncated, or it plainly reacts to something other than this task.

`unclear` is not for "the user did not express an opinion." Most users never do; that is `satisfied`.

Judge only whether the ORIGINAL REQUEST was satisfied — not the quality or difficulty of any new request.

When you are on the fence, choose `satisfied`. A missed complaint is a small loss; a false accusation is a large one.

## Output

Respond with ONLY a JSON object, filling the steps in order:
{"delivered": "≤15 words naming the thing produced", "complaint_quote": "words copied verbatim from the follow-up, or empty string", "quote_targets_delivered": true | false, "same_failure_or_pushback": true | false, "verdict": "satisfied" | "not_satisfied" | "unclear", "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low", "evidence": "≤15 words"}

`verdict` must be `not_satisfied` if and only if (`complaint_quote` is non-empty AND `quote_targets_delivered` is true) OR `same_failure_or_pushback` is true — unless you answered `unclear`.

data.summaryContent:
<overview>
Synapse is a student study workspace combining notebooks, AI study tools, and time management. The latest request is to refine dashboard controls, simplify navigation, make YouTube links produce study transcripts, and redesign Tasks; changes are underway, with YouTube transcript retrieval still requiring a fix and the latest edits not yet validated.
</overview>

<history>
1. The user established Synapse’s vision: a free study workspace for students with document ingestion, AI chat and study tools, and task planning.
   - Project directory: `C:\Users\HarshLocal\Desktop\synapse ai study website`.
   - The project uses Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind, Supabase, and Groq-related AI routes.

2. Earlier requests built the dashboard and study workflow, including source ingestion, chat, notes, flashcards, quizzes, theme support, and notebook persistence.
   - The user later requested a redesigned dashboard, task manager, notebook-specific module tabs, chat citations/actions, and removal of podcast/voice features.
   - Those changes were implemented in the preceding segment. TypeScript passed then; ESLint for dashboard still reported existing React setState-in-effect errors.

3. The current request asks to:
   - Make oversized round buttons fit their controls; remove Feedback and Upgrade.
   - Limit the sidebar to Home, Notebooks, Chat, and Tasks; show Notes, Flashcards, and Quiz only within an opened notebook.
   - Import YouTube video transcripts directly, without asking for a separate text file, and avoid adding a paid API.
   - Make the Tasks interface more professional.

4. Current changes in progress:
   - Removed the global `border-radius: 9999px !important` rule that forced every button into a pill, and retained pill shapes only on appropriate controls.
   - Removed Feedback and Upgrade from the dashboard header and reduced sidebar navigation to four items.
   - Reworked Tasks with a summary row, labeled task-creation fields, cleaner status controls, and responsive styling.
   - Added a YouTube captions attempt in the existing ingest route, using public YouTube caption tracks without adding a package or paid provider.
   - Tested that approach against a public captioned video: YouTube returned the page and caption-track metadata, but the timed-text request returned an empty body. The latest work therefore is **not complete**; use the YouTube InnerTube `get_transcript` endpoint or correct the timed-text request before calling this done.
</history>
<work_done>
**Files modified in the current request**
- `src/app/dashboard/dashboard-home.tsx`
  - Sidebar navigation is now Home, Notebooks, Chat, and Tasks.
  - Header Feedback and Upgrade buttons and their dialog state/markup were removed.
  - Task view was redesigned with task counts, a date pill, labeled creation fields, and improved task rows.
  - YouTube submit now calls the ingest endpoint and creates a notebook from the returned transcript.
  - A shared notebook-creation helper is used for uploaded files and YouTube transcripts.

- `src/app/globals.css`
  - Removed the blanket forced-round button styling.
  - Added scoped sizing/radius rules, redesigned task styling, and responsive layouts.

- `src/app/api/study/ingest/route.ts`
  - Added YouTube URL parsing and public caption-track retrieval, without an extra dependency.
  - Current timed-text implementation returns empty transcript data in the real-world probe; it needs correction.

**Prior changes still in the worktree**
- `src/app/dashboard/dashboard-home.tsx`, `src/app/globals.css`, `src/app/landing-client.tsx`, `src/app/api/study/chat/route.ts`, and `src/lib/study/groq.ts` also contain the earlier dashboard redesign, task persistence, citation actions, and podcast/audio removal.
- The workspace was already dirty with unrelated user changes. Do not revert them.

**Validation**
- Before the latest request, `tsc --noEmit` passed.
- Dashboard ESLint reported two existing React `setState`-inside-effect errors and warnings; lint for landing and changed server routes had passed then.
- **No type-check, lint, build, or diff check has been run after the current edits.**
- No dependency was installed and no live deployment or Supabase migration was performed.
</work_done>
<technical_details>
- Project path: `C:\Users\HarshLocal\Desktop\synapse ai study website`.
- Stack observed previously: Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3, TypeScript 5, Tailwind 4.
- The project’s `AGENTS.md` requires reading Next.js documentation before Next.js changes. The Route Handler guide was previously read at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/03-api-reference/03-file-conventions/route.md`.
- YouTube probe used the public video `aircAruvnKk` (“But what is a neural network?”). The watch page exposed `ytInitialPlayerResponse`, 31 caption tracks, and an English track, but the `timedtext` endpoint returned HTTP 200 with an empty body.
- The same page contained `getTranscriptEndpoint` in its initial data. A GitHub code search also found implementations using `/youtubei/v1/get_transcript`; inspect that approach next, extracting its `params` from YouTube page data and passing the page’s Innertube API key/context. The precise response shape has not yet been examined.
- Public captions require that the video has captions enabled and is accessible. A truly free method cannot guarantee a transcript for videos without captions; don’t claim universal availability. Local video transcription still uses the existing Groq route/configuration and its provider quota.
- Do not inspect or disclose `.env.local` or credentials.
</technical_details>
<important_files>
- `src/app/dashboard/dashboard-home.tsx`
  - Current task/navigation/UI work and client-side `importYouTubeSource`.
  - The shared `createNotebookFromSource` helper handles Supabase/local persistence.
  - Review near `createNotebookFromSource`, `importYouTubeSource`, the Tasks branch, sidebar navigation, and YouTube form.

- `src/app/api/study/ingest/route.ts`
  - New YouTube helper code near the top: `getYouTubeVideoId` and `fetchYouTubeTranscript`.
  - `POST` handles a `youtubeUrl` form field before file-upload handling.
  - The current timed-text extraction is the known failing portion; use `getTranscriptEndpoint`/InnerTube or correct the timed-text query and verify with a captioned public video.

- `src/app/globals.css`
  - Current task interface styling and scoped button sizing are appended near the end.
  - The global border-radius override was removed; check the relevant base and latest task rules for unintended shape or sizing regressions.

- `src/app/api/study/chat/route.ts`
  - Earlier citation implementation adds numbered source chunks for chat responses and returns citation excerpts.

- `src/app/landing-client.tsx`
  - Earlier podcast/audio demo, feature card, comparison row, and FAQ were removed.
</important_files>
<next_steps>
1. Fix YouTube transcript extraction.
